chunks: Among them is Jalhama ibn Adad ibn Zaid ibn Yashjab ibn Arib ibn Zaid ibn Kahlan ibn Yarab,
and he is called Tai, and all of Tai are traced back to him, and his story is long to explain.
And he had a nephew called Yahabir ibn Malik ibn Adad,
and each of them had lived five hundred years.
A dispute occurred between them regarding pasture land.
So Jalhama feared the destruction of his clan.
He left it and traveled through the stages (of journey).
And he was the owner of Aja and Salma, two mountains in Tai.
And his story is long and well-known.

key_terms.أَجَأَ: Aja, one of the two mountains associated with Jalhama
key_terms.جَلْهَمَةُ: Jalhama, an ancestor of the Tai tribe
key_terms.سَلْمَى: Salma, one of the two mountains associated with Jalhama

ai.seo_question: Who was Jalhama and how did the Tai tribe get its name?
ai.summary: This narrative from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* highlights the pre-Islamic Arab lineage of Jalhama, emphasizing the concept of *karamat* (miraculous traits) and extended lifespans common in early Arab history. The etymological link to the Tai tribe and the specific geography of Aja and Salma mountains ground this account in tribal historiography, illustrating how oral traditions preserve genealogical and geographical memory alongside spiritual significance.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: Another long-lived ruler of Arabs was Jalhama bin Adad bin Zaid bin Yashjab bin Arib bin Zaid bin Kahlan bin Yarab.
He is also known as Lajalmaha Tai and Bani Tai are his descendants. His account is very long.
Yahabir bin Malik bin Adad was one of his nephews.
Each of them lived for 500 years
and there was a battle between them regarding a pasture land.
Jalhama thought that in this way his whole clan will be destroyed.
So he left that place and traveled a great distance;
that is why he began to be called as Tai.
He was the owner of two mountains in Tai, named Aja and Salma.
He is also having a very lengthy account.
